passages.title: A School Career Day
passages.text:
Our school career day takes place in the main hall, which is divided into several practical areas. Near the entrance, a notice board lists the schedule and the names of visiting speakers. Along the left wall, local colleges display information about study programmes, scholarships, and admission requirements. On the opposite side, several companies have set up small booths where students can ask about entry-level jobs and internships.

At the centre of the hall, a career guidance desk offers short conversations with teachers and invited advisers. Students can bring a draft CV, ask how to describe their skills, or discuss which subjects may support a future plan. A quiet corner is reserved for short practice interviews, while a computer station lets students search official college and company websites.

The atmosphere is busy but supportive. Some students arrive with a clear goal, whereas others are still exploring possibilities. The organisers remind everyone that career day is not a recruitment test and that students do not need to make a final decision immediately. Its purpose is to help them compare options, ask informed questions, and identify a useful next step.

passages.title: Taking the Bus Around the City
passages.text:
The city bus terminal is organised to make journeys easier for different passengers. Large route boards hang above the waiting area, showing each route number, its main stops, and the estimated departure time. Digital screens display updates when a bus is delayed, while printed maps remain available for people who prefer a paper guide. Benches are arranged in rows, leaving a clear path toward the boarding gates.

A separate sign marks the accessible boarding point. Buses on several routes have low floors and reserved spaces for passengers who use wheelchairs or need extra time to board. Staff members are usually stationed near the information desk, where passengers can ask about transfers or report a lost item. Ticket machines accept electronic payments, and a counter is available for people who need help using them.

The system is not perfect. During rush hour, some buses become crowded, and a digital update may appear later than expected. Still, clear signs and staff support help passengers plan their trips with greater confidence. For new users, checking the route before joining a queue is especially useful because buses leaving from nearby gates may travel in different directions.
hints: checking the route before joining a queue

passages.title: My First Week as a Part-Time Shop Assistant
passages.text:
During the school holiday, I worked for one week as a part-time assistant at a small stationery shop near my house. On the first morning, the owner showed me where to find notebooks, pens, folders, and art supplies. I thought the job would be easy because I often visited the shop as a customer, but I soon realised that serving customers required more attention than I expected. 

On my second day, a customer asked whether a particular notebook was available in a larger size. I checked the shelf quickly and told her that we did not sell it. The owner later showed me that the larger notebooks were kept in a drawer under the counter. I felt embarrassed, but she explained that I should check the storage area before giving an answer. She also reminded me to speak politely even when the shop became busy. 

By the middle of the week, I had learned to arrange returned items, check price labels, and ask a co-worker when I was unsure. One afternoon, several customers arrived at the same time. Instead of rushing, I greeted each person and explained that I would help them in turn. The owner said I was becoming more careful and organised. 

When the week ended, I was tired but pleased with what I had learned. I understood that customer service was not only about being friendly; it also required accurate information, patience, and knowing when to ask for help. The experience did not make me an expert, but it gave me more confidence about trying another part-time job in the future.
hints: knowing when to ask for help

passages.title: How Our Neighborhood Fixed a Flooded Road
passages.text:
After heavy rain, the road beside our neighbourhood market often filled with water. Pedestrians had to step into traffic to pass the deepest part, and some motorcyclists lost their balance on the uneven edge. At first, residents complained in separate messages, but the problem continued because the reports did not show exactly where the water collected or how long it remained.

One Saturday, our youth group decided to document the situation. We took photographs from safe positions, noted the time and rainfall conditions, and marked the worst section on a simple map. An adult volunteer helped us send the information to the local service office. We did not try to open the drain ourselves because the water was dirty and the roadside was unsafe.

A few days later, workers inspected the drain and found it partly blocked by leaves and plastic packaging. They cleared the blockage and arranged a follow-up check after the next rain. The road still flooded slightly during an unusually heavy shower, but the water disappeared more quickly than before. Residents continued to report rubbish near the drain, and shop owners placed a bin near the market entrance. We learned that useful community action requires clear evidence, cooperation, and realistic expectations rather than complaints alone.
hints: reports did not show exactly where

passages.title: Jaka Tarub and Nawang Wulan
passages.text:
One day, a young man named Jaka Tarub was walking near a forest when he heard laughter beside a hidden pool. He looked through the trees and saw several heavenly maidens bathing there. Their shawls, which allowed them to return to the sky, lay on the grass nearby. Jaka Tarub secretly took one shawl and hid it. When the maidens finished bathing, one of them could not find hers and was unable to return with the others. Her name was Nawang Wulan.

Jaka Tarub approached her and offered help. With no way to return home, Nawang Wulan eventually lived with him, and they married. Before long, they had a daughter. Nawang Wulan had a special ability: she could cook enough rice for the family from a small amount of grain, but she made Jaka Tarub promise never to open the rice container while she was cooking.

For a long time, he kept the promise. One day, however, he became curious and lifted the lid. He discovered the hidden shawl inside the container, where Nawang Wulan had kept it safe. After that, her special ability disappeared, and she had to cook in an ordinary way. When the rice ran low, she searched the storage area and found her shawl. Realising that Jaka Tarub had taken it, she understood how he had kept her from returning home. In many tellings, she eventually leaves for the sky, while their daughter remains connected to both parents. The story is often remembered as a warning that deception can damage trust even when a relationship seems happy.
hints: promise never to open the rice container

passages.title: The Legend of Cindelaras
passages.text:
Long ago, in a kingdom in East Java, a queen gave birth to a boy named Cindelaras. The king’s other wife was jealous and wanted her own son to become the heir. She persuaded a palace servant to spread a false accusation against the queen. Believing the story without checking it carefully, the king ordered the queen to leave the palace. She went to live in a forest, where she raised Cindelaras far from court life.

As Cindelaras grew older, he became brave and curious. One day, he found an egg and cared for it until a strong rooster hatched. The rooster became known for its unusual crow, which seemed to announce that Cindelaras was the son of a king. People who heard the crow told others about it, and the story eventually reached the palace.

When the king heard the reports, he invited Cindelaras to prove the claim. In a traditional rooster contest, Cindelaras’s bird defeated the king’s champion. The king then asked about the boy’s family, and the truth about the false accusation came to light. The queen was welcomed back, and the people learned that rumours can cause serious harm when leaders accept them without evidence. Different versions of the legend vary in detail, but the rooster’s crow and the discovery of Cindelaras’s identity are central to this retelling.

passages.title: How to Make a Monthly Budget
passages.text:
A monthly budget helps you decide how to use the money you receive instead of wondering where it went at the end of the month. Begin by listing your expected income, such as pocket money, wages from part-time work, or money earned from a small service. Use the amount you can reasonably expect, not an uncertain amount you hope to receive.

Next, write down necessary expenses, including transport, meals, phone data, and school supplies. Estimate each amount using recent spending records if possible. Then set aside a realistic amount for savings or an unexpected cost before deciding how much is available for non-essential purchases. If your expenses are higher than your income, identify which flexible costs can be reduced; do not simply remove an important need from the list.

For the rest of the month, record each purchase as it happens. A note on your phone or a small notebook is enough. At the end of the week, compare your actual spending with your plan and make adjustments if needed. A budget is a guide, not a punishment: if an unexpected expense appears, update the figures rather than pretending the original plan still works. After one month, review which estimates were accurate and use that information to prepare the next budget.

passages.title: How to Choose a Reliable Source for an Essay
passages.text:
When you write an essay, a source should do more than sound convincing. Start by identifying who created the information. Look for the author’s name, relevant experience, or the organisation responsible for the page. If the author cannot be identified, treat the claim cautiously rather than assuming it is false or automatically true.

Next, examine the evidence. A reliable source explains where its facts come from, uses examples or data that can be checked, and separates evidence from personal opinion. Check the publication date too, especially when the topic involves technology, public policy, or current statistics. An older source may still explain a historical event well, but it may not describe a recent change.

Then consider the purpose of the text. Is it trying to inform readers, sell a product, or persuade them to support a particular view? A persuasive purpose does not make a source useless, but it means you should notice what information is emphasised or left out. Finally, compare the main claim with at least one independent source. If several sources repeat the same statement but all refer to one original post, they do not provide fully independent confirmation. Keep a record of the title, author, date, and link so you can cite the source accurately in your essay.

passages.title: Should Students Use AI for Schoolwork?
passages.text:
Students should be allowed to use artificial intelligence tools for some school tasks, but the tools must support learning rather than replace it. AI can help learners generate practice questions, organise early ideas, or receive explanations of unfamiliar concepts. Used carefully, it can give students another way to explore a topic before asking a teacher for further guidance.

However, a fluent answer is not necessarily an accurate one. AI tools can make mistakes, leave out important context, or produce information that sounds certain without adequate evidence. If students submit generated work as if they had written and checked every part themselves, teachers cannot easily see what the students actually understand. The students may also miss the thinking process that helps them remember and apply knowledge.

Schools should therefore teach clear rules for responsible use. Students can be asked to verify important claims, acknowledge when AI has contributed to an assignment, and explain their own reasoning. Teachers can design tasks that include drafts, source checks, or short reflections, making the learning process more visible. Some activities should still be completed without AI so students practise independent skills. The goal is not to ban every tool or accept every answer, but to use technology with honesty, judgement, and accountability.
hints: support learning rather than replace it

passages.title: Why Students Need Public Transportation
passages.text:
Reliable public transportation can make education and work more accessible. When buses and other shared services connect residential areas with schools, training centres, and workplaces, people who cannot drive have more choices. A predictable route can also help families plan their day without paying for a separate private journey every time someone needs to travel.

Public transport may reduce the number of private vehicles on busy roads, especially when services are frequent and convenient. Fewer cars can mean less pressure on parking spaces and potentially lower traffic emissions. It can also give teenagers and older residents more independence, provided that stops are safe and routes are easy to understand.

Nevertheless, public transportation is not a complete solution by itself. Some areas have limited service, and infrequent buses may force passengers to wait a long time or use another vehicle for part of the journey. Poor lighting, crowded stops, and unclear information can also discourage people from using the system. Local authorities should therefore improve route coverage, maintain vehicles, publish clear schedules, and listen to passenger feedback. Public transport works best when it is affordable, dependable, and designed around the needs of the people who use it.

To prove that every old source is unreliable
To confirm that the source was written to sell a product
To avoid checking the evidence in the source
questions.why: The passage says the date matters especially for technology, public policy, and current statistics; older sources may not describe recent changes.
questions.evidence: “Check the publication date too, especially when the topic involves technology, public policy, or current statistics.”
wrong: The length of an author’s name is irrelevant to reliability.
Correct: dates help readers judge whether information is current enough for the topic.
The passage explicitly says an older source may still explain a historical event well.
Purpose is checked separately; the date does not establish that a source sells a product.
Date-checking does not replace checking evidence; the procedure recommends both.

questions.stem: Which TWO actions are recommended when evaluating a source for an essay? Select TWO answers.
options: Skip recording source details once the essay draft is complete.
Check whether its evidence can be verified.
Compare its main claim with an independent source.
Treat every persuasive source as automatically useless.
Assume several sites provide independent proof even if they copy one post.
questions.why: The procedure recommends checking verifiable evidence and comparing the claim with at least one independent source.
questions.evidence: “uses examples or data that can be checked” and “compare the main claim with at least one independent source.”
wrong: It recommends recording the title, author, date, and link for accurate citation.
Supported: verifiability is a stated sign of reliability.
Supported: independent comparison helps check a claim.
The passage says persuasive purpose does not automatically make a source useless.
The passage warns that repeated copies of one original post are not independent confirmation.

rows.s: Compare the main statement with independent reporting.
rows.why: This tests whether the claim is supported beyond one source.

rows.s: Record the publication date and the link.

questions.stem: What is the writer’s main position on AI in schoolwork?
options: A generated answer is reliable whenever it sounds confident.
All school tasks should be completed with AI to save time.
Students should never learn how to use AI tools.
AI can be useful if students use it transparently and continue thinking independently.
AI should replace teachers whenever it gives a fluent answer.
questions.why: The writer supports limited, responsible use while warning against errors and recommending verification, acknowledgement, and some AI-free tasks.
questions.evidence: “Students should be allowed to use ... tools for some school tasks, but the tools must support learning rather than replace it.”
wrong: The passage warns that AI may sound certain without adequate evidence.
The writer says some activities should be completed without AI.
The writer supports teaching clear rules for responsible use, not banning all use.
Correct: it captures the balanced position in the introduction and conclusion.
The passage does not suggest replacing teachers and warns that fluent answers can be wrong.

questions.stem: Which TWO practices are consistent with the writer’s recommendations? Select TWO answers.
options: Allow AI to make every decision about what students understand.
Use AI to avoid explaining one’s own reasoning.
Submit generated text without checking it if it sounds fluent.
Acknowledge when AI has contributed to an assignment.
Verify important claims produced with AI.
questions.why: The writer recommends checking important claims and acknowledging AI contributions so students remain accountable for their work.
questions.evidence: “Students can be asked to verify important claims, acknowledge when AI has contributed to an assignment, and explain their own reasoning.”
wrong: The passage says teachers need to see what students understand; AI cannot replace that judgement.
The writer says students should explain their own reasoning.
The passage warns that fluent answers may be inaccurate and should be checked.
Supported: transparent acknowledgement is explicitly recommended.
Supported: verification is explicitly recommended.

rows.s: Submitting generated work as one’s own can hide what the student understands.
rows.why: This risk makes learning and assessment less transparent.
rows.otherCategoryWhy: Not Benefit: this statement concerns risk rather than benefit.

rows.s: AI can explain unfamiliar concepts in another way.
rows.why: The passage identifies explanations as a possible learning support.
rows.otherCategoryWhy: Not Risk: this statement concerns benefit rather than risk.

rows.s: A fluent answer may contain errors or missing context.
rows.why: This is a limitation of AI-generated information.
rows.otherCategoryWhy: Not Benefit: this statement concerns risk rather than benefit.

rows.s: AI can generate practice questions for learners.
rows.why: This is presented as a way AI can support learning.
rows.otherCategoryWhy: Not Risk: this statement concerns benefit rather than risk.

questions.why: The first two statements describe possible learning benefits; the last two describe risks of inaccurate or untransparent use.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how can public transportation improve access to education and work?
options: It connects residential areas with schools, training centres, and workplaces.
It makes private vehicles illegal on busy roads.
It guarantees that every neighbourhood has frequent service.
It removes the need for safe stops and clear route information.
It ensures that every passenger reaches a destination without transfers.
questions.why: The opening paragraph explains that connections between residential areas and key destinations give people who cannot drive more choices.
questions.evidence: “When buses and other shared services connect residential areas with schools, training centres, and workplaces, people who cannot drive have more choices.”
wrong: Correct: this is the main access benefit described.
No ban on private vehicles is proposed.
The passage later notes that some areas have limited service.
The passage says safe stops and easy-to-understand routes are important.
The passage notes that some journeys may require another vehicle for part of the trip.

questions.stem: Which TWO improvements does the writer recommend for public transportation? Select TWO answers.
options: Publish clear schedules and listen to passenger feedback.
Replace all buses with private cars.
Improve route coverage and maintain vehicles.
Keep service information unclear to prevent crowding.
Reduce the number of stops so buses can ignore less busy areas.
questions.why: The conclusion calls for better coverage, vehicle maintenance, clear schedules, and passenger feedback.
questions.evidence: “Local authorities should therefore improve route coverage, maintain vehicles, publish clear schedules, and listen to passenger feedback.”
wrong: Supported: schedules and passenger feedback are listed.
The passage discusses shared services as useful; it does not propose replacing them with private cars.
Supported: both route coverage and maintenance are listed.
The passage recommends clear information, not less clarity.
This conflicts with the recommendation to improve route coverage.

rows.s: Fewer private vehicles may reduce pressure on parking spaces.
rows.why: The passage describes this as a possible benefit.
rows.otherCategoryWhy: Not Limit: this statement concerns benefit rather than limit.

rows.s: Poor lighting and unclear information can discourage passengers.
rows.why: These are barriers that may reduce use.
rows.otherCategoryWhy: Not Benefit: this statement concerns limit rather than benefit.
